content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors propose an algorithm called  D-CIPHER to elicit differential  equations from data.  Authors also propose a new optimization procedure called CoLLie, to help D-CIPHER. Empirical examples are provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:


Authors have a good grasp of some of the challenges of eliciting differential equations from data. They have also planned the scope of the problem carefully, as can be evidenced from the notions like such as evolution form, evolution assumption, derivative-bound part, and derivative-free part, variational-ready PDE. 

Weakness:

The paper is one of bunch of definitions and some empirical analysis. It is not clear that the algorithm D-CIPHER can get past some of the major challenges with eliciting PDEs from data. Essentially, PDE estimation depends on the smooth function used to interpolate between observed data, and hence effectively depends on uncountable imputations between observations. Consequently, the estimated PDE (by any algorithm) tends to be heavily assumption dependent and extremely sensitive to noise. This issue has been deeply studied in the applied math literature and related machine learning literature, but the authors do not seem to be aware of this. The details in the supplementary materials also do not provide any theoretical results or hint that the algorithm indeed provides a consistent estimate of a PDE. I am surprised to find no discussion on or constraints and caveats based on signal to noise ratio, or chaotic systems and other well-known difficult/impossible cases of PDEs.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer HGvL [3/3]
content.comment:
## Noise, error bounds, limitations

### Noise
We have investigated empirically how our method performs in scenarios with different noise settings. Predictably, we observe that the performance deteriorates when the noise is higher but is still more robust than other methods.

### Error bounds
While we would like to have error bounds for the discovered PDE, we note that the problem we solve is significantly more difficult than the one considered in other works. The space of PDEs we consider is much more complex than the space of PDEs in a linear combination form. In other works (e.g.,  Rudy et al. (2017), Messenger & Bortz (2021)), the PDE is basically a vector in $\mathbb{R}^P$ and the discovery task is mostly reduced to finding a sparse enough vector that approximately solves a certain linear equation. Of course, there is a lot of literature that aids in establishing error bounds in such problem settings. However, D-CIPHER searches over a space $\mathbb{R}^P \times CFE(M+N)$, where $CFE(M+N)$ is a space of closed-form expressions in $M+N$ variables. This space is combinatorial in the functional form and continuous in real constants. This makes it very challenging to derive any error bounds.

### Limitations
We have discussed the limitations of our work in Section 8.

We hope that we have addressed all your comments. Please let us know if there is anything else you would like us to address.

## References
Chen, R. T., Rubanova, Y., Bettencourt, J. & Duvenaud, D. K. Neural ordinary differential equations. _Advances in neural information processing systems_ **31**, (2018).

Long, Z., Lu, Y. & Dong, B. PDE-Net 2.0: Learning PDEs from data with a numeric-symbolic hybrid deep network. _Journal of Computational Physics_ **399**, 108925 (2019).

Qian, Z., Kacprzyk, K. & van der Schaar, M. D-CODE: Discovering Closed-form ODEs from Observed Trajectories. _ICLR_ (2022).

Rudy, S. H., Brunton, S. L., Proctor, J. L. & Kutz, J. N. Data-driven discovery of partial differential equations. _Sci. Adv._ **3**, e1602614 (2017).

Messenger, D. A. & Bortz, D. M. Weak SINDy for partial differential equations. _J. Comp. Phy._ **443**, 110525 (2021).

Brunton, S. L., Proctor, J. L. & Kutz, J. N. Discovering governing equations from data by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamical systems. _Proc Natl Acad Sci USA_ **113**, 3932–3937 (2016).

Kaheman, K., Kutz, J. N. & Brunton, S. L. SINDy-PI: a robust algorithm for parallel implicit sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics. _Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences_ **476**, 20200279 (2020).

content.title: Reply to Reviewer HGvL [2/3]
content.comment:
## Comparison with Qian et al. (2022)
To clarify our contributions, we compare D-CIPHER to algorithm in Qian et al. (2022) (recently published at ICLR 2022) which we think is closest in spirit to the algorithm we developed as both of them allow any closed-form derivative-free part and use variational formulation to circumvent derivative estimation. We also note how the new notions we introduce help us compare the two works.

The algorithm in Qian et al. (2022) can discover any first-order explicit closed-form ODE, i.e., an equation of the form.
$$ \partial_t u_j(t) = g(\textbf{u}(t),t) $$
where $g$ is a closed-form function. It uses the variational formulation of ODEs to circumvent derivative estimation.

| Property | Qian et al. (2022) | D-CIPHER |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Applicable to PDEs | No | Yes |
| Higher-order derivatives | No (only first-order) | Yes |
| Requires evolution assumption | Yes | No |
| Derivative-bound part | Fixed: $\partial_t u_j$ | Learned: $\sum_{p=1}^P \beta_p \hat{\mathcal{E}}_p[\textbf{u}]$ |
| Derivative-free part | Any closed-form function | Any closed-form function |
| Derivative estimation | No | No |
Qian et al. (2022) can be considered a special case of D-CIPHER. We can recover it from D-CIPHER by choosing the dictionary to contain only one element, i.e., $\mathcal{Q} = \{\partial_t u_j\}$.

As the derivative-bound part is fixed, every ODE of that form admits the variational formulation. This is not true for PDEs as there are derivative-bound parts that might prohibit the variational formulation. Thus D-CIPHER required careful consideration of the appropriate class of equations to search over.

As D-CIPHER needs to find both the $\partial$-free part (function $g$) and the $\partial$-bound part, the optimization problem is much more complicated. That is why we restrict the derivative-bound part of the PDE to be spanned by terms from the pre-specified dictionary and develop an efficient optimization algorithm, CoLLie. We emphasize that, as is the case for Qian et al. (2022), we do not put any constraints on the derivative-free part of the PDE, apart from it being closed-form. 

## Challenges of PDE discovery
We agree that PDE discovery is a very difficult task with many challenges. In this work, we tried to address some of them. We have added Appendix F.6 containing a table outlining some of the challenges of PDE discovery and how we address them. We reproduce it below.

| Challenge | Novel contribution (how we address the challenge) |
| -- | -- |
| Noisy measurements | We use the variational loss function (Equation 10) |
| Large diversity of PDEs | We allow any closed-form derivative-free part and require no evolution assumption (Section 2)|
| Learning compact equations | We penalize long derivative-free parts and use L1 normalization for the $\partial$-bound part (Section 5, Appendix E.3)|
| Efficient search | We develop a quick algorithm, CoLLie, for the inner optimization (Section 6) |
| Chaotic systems | We do *not* estimate the initial conditions (Chen et al., 2018) or perform forward time stepping (Long et al., 2019) which are computationally unstable for chaotic systems |

As you mentioned PDE discovery (by any algorithm) is assumption dependent and sensitive to noise. In our work, we tried to address these challenges by
-   Allowing any closed-form derivative-free part of the equation and not requiring the evolution assumption
-   Using the variational formulation of PDE that is more robust to noisy data than derivative estimation. (We investigated the issues of derivative estimation in Appendix F.5)

content.title: Reply to Reviewer HGvL [1/3]
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer HGvL,

Thank you for your time and insightful comments.

## Theoretical contributions
In this section, we want to justify that the new notions we introduce (evolution assumption, linear combination form, derivative-bound part, derivative-fee part, Variational-Ready PDEs) are important theoretical contributions that help us understand the landscape of different PDEs from the machine learning perspective.

The definitions we introduce let us characterize different classes of PDEs. These new notions complement the standard recognized PDE classes such as semi-linear, quasilinear, hyperbolic, etc. These standard classes were introduced predominantly to characterize the solving techniques or the properties of the solutions, whereas the notions we introduce relate to the difficulty of discovering such equations from data. 

### Significance of linear combination form and the evolution assumption

In the table below we demonstrate how the presence of the two assumptions, the linear combination form (LC) and the evolution assumption (EA), influences the optimization problem.

| LC | EA | Equation form | Optimization problem | Examples |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| Yes | Yes | $\partial_t u_j = \sum_{p=1}^P q_p f_p(\textbf{x},\textbf{u}(\textbf{x}),\partial^{[K]}\textbf{u}(\textbf{x}))$ | Relatively easy. Can be formulated as finding sparse solution to linear least squares (similar to ridge regression) | Brunton et al. (2016), Rudy et al. (2017) |
| Yes | No | $\sum_{p=1}^P q_p f_p(\textbf{x},\textbf{u}(\textbf{x}),\partial^{[K]}\textbf{u}(\textbf{x})) = 0$ | Medium difficulty. Can be formulated as $P$ separate linear least squares problems as above | Kaheman et al. (2020) |
| No | Yes | $\partial_t u_j = g(\textbf{x},\textbf{u}(x))$ | Medium difficulty. Find $g$ using symbolic regression | Qian et al. (2022) |
| No | No | $f(\textbf{x},\textbf{u}(\textbf{x}),\partial^{[K]}\textbf{u}(\textbf{x})) = 0$ | Very difficult. Requires other assumptions (in this work, Equation 12) | D-CIPHER | 

We see that with both assumptions, the problem is relatively straightforward and reduces to sparse linear regression. With only one of the assumptions present the problem becomes more difficult. With neither of these assumptions, the problem becomes very difficult and requires some other assumptions. D-CIPHER does not make either of these assumptions but it assumes the PDE to be of the form described by Equation 12.

### Significance of $\partial$-bound part, $\partial$-free part and Variational-Ready PDEs
The difficulty of derivative estimation has been of the main challenges of PDE discovery (Rudy et al., 2017). The variational formulation allows to circumvent derivative estimation and thus is more robust to noisy data. We observed that any restrictions that the variational formulation might put on the equation come from the terms containing the derivatives. Thus we define the derivative-bound part and the derivative-free part of the PDE due to their significance for the variational formulation. That allows us to define Variational-Ready PDEs as currently the broadest class of PDEs that admit the variational formulation. We believe it is an important contribution as methods requiring derivative estimation underperform in settings with high noise. This definition outlines the current limits of any method that circumvents derivative estimation in that way.

### Justification of the loss function
Theorem 1 which is stated in Section 4 and proved in Appendix B.2 proves the variational characterization of VR-PDEs, i.e., the expression in Equation 9 is 0 if and only if the corresponding PDE is true. Moreover, it implies that our loss function (Equation 13) is minimized by a correct PDE.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer HS33 [2/2]
content.comment:
## Answers
In this section, we directly answer your questions one by one.

Question:
>“For example, to discover the last four equations in Table 4, why original loss does not work? Is the proposed variational objective function necessary to discover this kind of PDE or just for optimization robustness?”

Answer: 
The last four equations are not in a linear combination form (Equation 4) as marked by the x mark in the column "LC" in Table 2. Thus they *cannot* be discovered by previous methods that assume such form (discussed in Sections 2 and 3). These equations *can* be discovered by D-CIPHER because it makes no assumption on the derivative-free part of the equation apart from being closed-form (as described in Section 5). The variational formulation is not strictly necessary for the discovery of these equations but it dramatically improves the performance as shown in Sec 7.2 (Figure 3, Table 3, Figure 4) where we compare D-CIPHER with its ablated version that does not use the variational formulation but the standard MSE loss (Equation 57).

Question: Robustness in discovering higher-order differential equations.

Answer:
Estimating derivatives from data is challenging and the higher the order of the derivative the less accurate it becomes. We have investigated this issue and added Appendix F.5 which demonstrates this phenomenon. Previous methods (e.g., (Rudy et al., 2017)) need to estimate the derivatives as they do not use the variational formulation. In D-CIPHER, instead of estimating the derivatives of the observed fields, we only have to calculate the derivates of pre-specified testing functions that we can calculate analytically without losing any precision even if we take higher-order derivatives. We have demonstrated that D-CIPHER can discover higher-order differential equations by successfully recovering the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation (Figure 2) which is a fourth-order PDE.

We assume that the dictionary contains the derivative-bound terms of the PDE we want to discover. This assumption is less strict than the one made in other works (e.g., (Rudy et al., 2017), (Messenger & Bortz, 2021)) that assume that the terms in the whole equation (both the derivative-bound and the derivative-free part) are contained in the dictionary. We have also demonstrated that our method performs well even when the dictionary is increased. In Appendix F.3, we show that the error does not increase when we enlarge the size of the dictionary $\mathcal{Q}$. We believe this is a direct result of normalizing using the L1 norm that is known to favor sparsity and to be less susceptible to a high number of features (here, elements of the dictionary).

Question: 
> “For example, the optimization procedure (CoLLie) is listed as a contribution in the introduction, however, there's no details about the algorithm in section 6.”

Answer:
Unfortunately, due to space limitations, we had to delegate the detailed description of CoLLie to Appendix D.

Question: 
> “For example, what is "Abi. D-CIPHER"?

Answer: 
We have mentioned that we compare D-CIPHER with its ablated version at the beginning of Section 7 and throughout Section 7.2. We have further improved the captions.

Question: 
> Why does some lines in Figure 2 disappear?

Answer: Unfortunately, some of the benchmarks are so close to each other that they overlap. We have already highlighted this issue in the figure caption and we have further improved the figure with proper annotations



We hope that we have addressed all your comments. Please let us know if there is anything else you would like us to address.

## References
Chen, R. T., Rubanova, Y., Bettencourt, J. & Duvenaud, D. K. Neural ordinary differential equations. _Advances in neural information processing systems_ **31**, (2018).

Long, Z., Lu, Y. & Dong, B. PDE-Net 2.0: Learning PDEs from data with a numeric-symbolic hybrid deep network. _Journal of Computational Physics_ **399**, 108925 (2019).

Qian, Z., Kacprzyk, K. & van der Schaar, M. D-CODE: Discovering Closed-form ODEs from Observed Trajectories. _The Tenth International Conference on Learning Representations_ (2022).

Rudy, S. H., Brunton, S. L., Proctor, J. L. & Kutz, J. N. Data-driven discovery of partial differential equations. _Sci. Adv._ **3**, e1602614 (2017).

Messenger, D. A. & Bortz, D. M. Weak SINDy for partial differential equations. _Journal of Computational Physics_ **443**, 110525 (2021).

content.title: Dear Reviewer HS33
content.comment:
Thank you for your response. Let us address your concern: "each proposed method is incremental and the challenges do not have a strong motivation in application". We structure our response into two sections, one addressing the motivations of challenges and clarifying why noise is a big issue in equation discovery, and the other addressing the issue of incrementality.


## Motivations of challenges

In this section, we demonstrate that the challenges we address have strong motivations.

### Noisy measurements
We define what we mean by a noisy measurement in Equation 11. The noise variable accounts for a random error inherent in any measurement. Noisy measurements are an important issue in any scientific or engineering field. Its importance gave rise to whole new areas of engineering that focus on noise reduction (Vaseghi, 2008).

Noise becomes an even bigger issue when derivative estimation is involved. As described in the seminal work (Rudy et al., 2017): 

> "Proper evaluation of the numerical derivatives is the most challenging and critical task for the success of the method. This is particularly true when the discretized solution contains measurement noise."

Based on your previous comments, we also performed our experiments to demonstrate that this problem becomes harder with higher-order derivatives. The results are in Appendix F.5. You can also see them [here](https://imgur.com/a/7Zwu9Bf).

### Chaotic systems
First, we want to point out that being "chaotic" and being "noisy" are two different things. That is why we classify them as two different challenges. It is possible to have data from a chaotic system without noise or noisy data from a non-chaotic system. Chaotic systems often appear in nature (double pendulum, fluid flow, climate, and weather modeling) and that is why it is important to have a method that is not susceptible to them.

## The novelty of D-CIPHER

We have already discussed the novelty of our method in the main text, appendix, and in our replies on this forum. In particular, we looked at it from the point of challenges of PDE discovery (Appendix F.6), by comparing it with related works (Section 3), and by directly contrasting it with a recent algorithm (Appendix F.8). In this section, we present two arguments that D-CIPHER is **not** incremental.

### Argument 1: D-CIPHER solves a new problem
As D-CIPHER does not assume the linear combination form (LC) or the evolution assumption (EA), the equation form it can discover is different than any other previous technique. That also means that the optimization problem it needs to solve is much harder than in previous techniques. And that is why we design a novel optimization algorithm to tackle it. We summarise how the presence of the two assumptions (LC and EA) influences the optimization problem in Appendix F.7.

D-CIPHER can discover PDEs with any closed-form derivative-free part. That is why it cannot be incremental with respect to any other PDE discovery algorithm that assumes that the equation is in a linear combination form.

D-CIPHER also cannot be incremental with respect to Qian et al. (2021) which can discover *only first-order ODEs*.

### Argument 2: D-CIPHER satisfies the criteria for novelty
Every discovery algorithm:
1. makes an assumption on the equation form
2. defines an objective function
3. introduces an optimization algorithm

Whether a method is incremental or not depends on how many of these attributes are novel and to what extent. In the table below we summarize that D-CIPHER works for equations of the form not considered by any previous algorithm, defines a novel objective function, and a new optimization algorithm.
| Attribute | D-CIPHER | Novel? | Reference in the paper |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Equation form | $\sum_{p=1}^P \beta_p \hat{\mathcal{E}}_p\[\textbf{u}\](\textbf{x}) - g(\textbf{x},\textbf{u}(\textbf{x})) = 0$ | Yes | Eq. 12 |
| Objective | $\min_{g} \min_{\beta_1 = 1}\sum_{d=1}^D \sum_{s=1}^S \left( \sum_{p=1}^P \mathcal{F}(\beta_p \hat{\mathcal{E}}_p,\hat{\textbf{u}}^{(d)},\phi_s)-\int g(\textbf{x},\hat{\textbf{u}}^{(d)}(\textbf{x}))\phi_s(\textbf{x}) d\textbf{x} \right)^2$| Yes | Eq. 13 |
| Optimization algorithm | CoLLie |Yes | Sec. 6 & App. D |


## References

Vaseghi, S. V. _Advanced Digital Signal Processing and Noise Reduction_. (John Wiley & Sons, 2008).

Qian, Z., Kacprzyk, K. & van der Schaar, M. D-CODE: Discovering Closed-form ODEs from Observed Trajectories. _The Tenth International Conference on Learning Representations_ (2022).

Rudy, S. H., Brunton, S. L., Proctor, J. L. & Kutz, J. N. Data-driven discovery of partial differential equations. _Sci. Adv._ **3**, e1602614 (2017).

content.title: Response to authors
content.comment:
Thanks for the detailed feedbacks and I think it is clearer than the presentation in the main paper. I hope the authors could re-organize the story, highlight the novelty as shown in responses and compare the property of the proposed method in a separate discussion section. To my understanding, the right logic is to first propose a key motivation, e.g., to deal with a different and important class of equations discovery problem, which could not be addressed by any existing method. Then the challenges could be introduced, e.g., noisy observations, and optimization efficiency. In the discussion part, the property such as chaotic, high-order derivatives could be discussed. But the current version merged these aspects together to make me hard to catch the key point and logic.  The current version takes a lot of space to introduce the derivation of the variational form. To my understanding, there are existing literatures to study variational form of PDEs, but it seems that there is no discussion on which part is borrowed from literature and why the new form of PDE requires the specially design on its variational form. Citations of literatures are required and it's better to leave more space to introduce some details about CoLLie.  

Because re-organization needs a major revision and lots of efforts, I will keep my score.

content.title: Dear Reviewer HS33
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed response and for taking the time to review our paper. We would like to provide a rationale for our exposition.

We introduce the two challenges, "Derivatives not observed" and "Strong assumptions and constrained search space", together because they are closely connected. We observe that variational formulation puts constraints only on the derivative-bound part of the PDE and thus allows an arbitrary closed-form derivative-free part - that expands the space of previously considered PDEs. Introducing this new class of equations without referencing the variational formulation would therefore lose some important context.

Additionally, we want to clarify that we do not derive the variational form in the main text of the paper. The proof of Theorem 1 can be found in Appendix B. Instead, we use the main text to define the new class of PDEs we aim to discover.

Thank you again for your feedback and for considering our paper. We appreciate your time.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a symbolic-regression encapsulating approach to discovery of partial differential equations and a heuristic approximate solver of the constrained least-squares problem arising from the definition of learning PDEs as an optimization problem. The approach is evaluated and compared with related approaches on 7 synthetic experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Well written
- Complete description of the problem and solution
- Comparative and in depth evaluation on multiple problems

Weaknesses:
- High-level abstract description
- Dependence on field estimation and SR algorithm not discussed sufficiently
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The work is presented clearly. The approach is novel and the description details allow for reproducibility of the approach. The authors claim that the code for the experimental design will be published upon acceptance.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work addresses an important problem in an area of symbolic regression that requires more attention, as approaches to discovery of PDEs are scarce and mainly developed as extensions to either standard SR methods or methods for learning equations for dynamical systems in the form of ordinary differential equations. I am not an expert in the area of PDEs, but the presented results look convincing. The approach is presented in a manner of framework where different modules can be chosen based on the problem at hand. That being said the effect of the choice of these modules at least in the context of the experimental evaluation in the manuscript deserve a more extensive treatment.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer 54d7
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer 54d7,

Thank you for your time and encouraging comments. 

## Diagram
We have added a diagram in Appendix C.3 (Figure 5) depicting how D-CIPHER works. We hope that this diagram (and the pseudocode in Appendix C.2) complement the description in the main text, making it less abstract and high-level. We hope it is now easier to understand how various parts of the algorithm work together.

## Dependence on field estimation
Thank you for your suggestion on testing D-CIPHER with different estimation algorithms. We have performed additional experiments and included them in Appendix F.10. We compared our implementation of D-CIPHER (that uses Gaussian Process regression) with implementations utilizing Nearest Point interpolation, Linear interpolation, and Cubic interpolation. We observe that the algorithms that produce smoother functions (Gaussian Process, Spline interpolation) perform better than algorithms that do not have such smoothness guarantees. We also want to emphasize that field estimation is a much simpler problem than derivative estimation which we demonstrate in Appendix F.5.

We hope that we have addressed all your comments. Please let us know if there is anything else you would like us to address.

content.title: Response
content.comment: Thank you for your response to my comments. I remain positive about this work.

content.title: Summary of revisions
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful comments and suggestions. We have revised the manuscript based on the reviews. 

We have added the following sections to the appendix
- Appendix C.3 includes a diagram showing how D-CIPHER works
- Appendix F.5 discusses challenges of derivative estimation
- Appendix F.6 discusses the challenges of PDE discovery and how we address them
- Appendix F.7 discusses the significance of the new notions we introduce
- Appendix F.8 compares D-CIPHER with Qian et al. (2022)
- Appendix F.9 discusses the challenge of establishing error bounds
- Appendix F.10 compares different field estimation algorithms

We have also improved figure captions in Section 7 and annotated Figure 2 to improve clarity.

All changes are marked in blue.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The authors propose a symbolic-regression approach to discovery of partial differential equations and a heuristic approximate solver. The approach is evaluated and compared with related approaches on 7 synthetic experiments. 

The paper received diverse reviews, with some major concerns on (1) unclear statement of the matching between key challenges in the space of PDE discovery and the proposed solutions (2) the discussions and comparison with the rich literature of variational forms of PDEs (3) unclear paper organization which weakens the presentation of the novelty and technical contributions, etc. The authors actually did a fairly good job in the rebuttal and in revising their paper. One of the reviewers raised his/her score from 3 to 5. However, the other reviewer who also gave a negative score (of 3) insisted that the paper quality can hardly be improved to above the bar by minor revisions. As a result, we do not think it is a good idea to accept the paper in its current form.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The paper received quite a few negative comments. Although the authors did a good job in their rebuttals and one of the reviewers actually raised his score, the new score is still negative and the other reviewer insisted on keep his/her original negative score.
